input:
A contract packaging firm operating 2 plants, with revenue of $104 million per year, is considering a phased scheduling-system installation beginning at Plant 2 and then holding the remaining plants until results from Plant 2 are reported. The operations director owns the scheduling programme. The evidence base consists of order records for 12 months and 13383 orders. Over the last two quarters, on-time delivery was 87%, compared with a target of 95%. Overtime cost was $1.7 million last year, an increase of 20% on the year before, while the order backlog has risen to 3.8 weeks from 1.7 weeks a year ago. Plant 2 accounts for 68% of late orders, which is why it is the proposed starting point. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $273k, whereas Plant 2 alone is quoted at $138k. An internal estimate, rather than a vendor figure, suggests that overtime at Plant 2 could be reduced by 15-20% in the first year. Taken together, the figures point to a delivery problem concentrated mainly in one part of the operation, although the estimate of overtime benefit remains internal and has not yet been demonstrated in operation.

It is also relevant that the proposal is not simply to buy the system at a lower initial cost. The sequence matters because the firm can learn whether scheduling changes affect delivery performance and overtime in the plant where the problem is most visible before committing the same approach elsewhere. The backlog increase and the missed delivery target provide the operational context, while the concentration of late orders provides the reason for a staged approach. At the same time, the evidence does not establish that scheduling is the only cause of late delivery, nor does it quantify how much of the backlog would be cleared by the system. The quoted prices establish the difference in initial scope, but the internal overtime estimate remains the least secure part of the case. The recommendation therefore links expansion to reported results instead of treating the estimate as proof, and the named owner gives the programme a single point of accountability for reporting those results.
target:
Install the scheduling system at Plant 2 first and hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported. The operations director owns the scheduling programme. The evidence base is order records for 12 months, covering 13383 orders at a contract packaging firm with 2 plants and revenue of $104 million per year.

On-time delivery over the last two quarters was 87%, against a target of 95%. Overtime cost was $1.7 million last year, up 20% on the year before. The order backlog stands at 3.8 weeks, against 1.7 weeks a year ago. Plant 2 accounts for 68% of late orders, so the delivery shortfall is concentrated rather than evenly spread across the firm.

A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $273k; Plant 2 alone is $138k. The lower initial commitment tests the programme where late orders are concentrated. An internal estimate, not a vendor figure, puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15-20% in the first year. That estimate is a benefit to verify from reported results, not a saving already established.

The staged decision separates installation from expansion. Initial installation tests whether scheduling changes delivery performance and overtime where late orders are concentrated; expansion depends on reported results rather than on the internal estimate alone. The evidence does not show that scheduling is the only cause of late delivery, and it does not quantify the backlog reduction the system will produce. Those limits do not weaken the case for a first installation at the point of concentration, but they fix the status of the expected benefit: an estimate to be tested. The owner class is named because the hold on the other plants requires a reported result, not an assumption that the first installation succeeded.
